# ABSTRACT SECURITY
**The Security Data Pipeline Platform.** Deliver enriched, normalized security events to any destination — in real time, at scale.

[abstract.security](https://abstract.security) · [Documentation](https://docs.abstractsecurity.app/docs/integrations/) · [Book a demo](https://abstract.security)

---
### Per-subscription app registrations, automated
Creates one Entra app registration per subscription for Abstract's Microsoft Graph and Microsoft 365 collection — app + service principal, **admin consent granted and verified**, client secret straight to Key Vault, Azure RBAC on the target subscription.

**Read this first — one manual step is unavoidable.** This workflow acts through a user-assigned managed identity that must already hold Microsoft Graph `Application.ReadWrite.All` and `AppRoleAssignment.ReadWrite.All`, consented by a **Global Administrator**. Nothing can automate that grant: an identity able to assign app roles can grant *itself* anything in the directory, so automating it would be a privilege-escalation hole. Run `scripts/Deploy-AbstractAppReg.sh -a Bootstrap` once per tenant, then come back here.

**Understand what "per subscription" really means.** Entra app registrations and their Graph permissions are **tenant**-level objects — Graph permissions cannot be scoped to a subscription. What this actually isolates per subscription is **Azure RBAC**. One app per subscription gives you separate credentials, separate RBAC and independent revocation; it does *not* partition Graph data access.

**Why a workflow and not Azure Policy.** Azure Policy cannot create Entra objects — a `DeployIfNotExists` policy deploys an ARM template, and app registrations are not ARM resources. The policy variant in `templates/policy/` works around that by deploying a privileged container into every subscription. This path keeps the tier-0 identity in **one** place, gives you a single run history as the audit trail, and costs nothing per subscription. Prefer it unless governance mandates that everything arrive via Policy.

**Verified against a live tenant (2026-08-03):** consent is confirmed by reading `appRoleAssignments` back from Graph, not by trusting the POST — so a shortfall returns HTTP 500 naming the exact count instead of silently leaving Abstract to hit 403s.

options.text: PREREQUISITE — the managed identity below must already have Graph Application.ReadWrite.All + AppRoleAssignment.ReadWrite.All with admin consent. Without it every run fails at the first Graph call. Create and consent it with: ./scripts/Deploy-AbstractAppReg.sh -a Bootstrap -g <this-resource-group>

basics.name: workflowName
basics.label: Workflow name
basics.toolTip: Name of the Logic App that performs the onboarding.

basics.name: identitySelector
basics.label: Graph-permissioned managed identity
basics.toolTip: The user-assigned managed identity created and consented by the Bootstrap step. Treat it as a tier-0 credential: it can grant itself any directory permission.

basics.name: keyVaultName
basics.label: Central Key Vault name
basics.toolTip: Existing vault that receives every generated client secret. Deliberately central rather than one vault per subscription — scattering tier-0 secrets across the estate is worse, not better. Grant the identity Key Vault Secrets Officer on it.

constraints.validationMessage: 3-24 chars, letters/numbers/hyphens, must start with a letter.

options.text: The vault must already exist and the identity needs write access to it. RBAC vault: grant Key Vault Secrets Officer. Access-policy vault: grant get/set/list on secrets. ./scripts/Deploy-AbstractAppReg.sh -a Grant -k <vault> detects which model the vault uses and does the right one.

elements.name: appNamePattern
elements.label: App display-name pattern
elements.toolTip: {sub} is replaced with the subscription ID. This is ALSO the idempotency key — the workflow reuses an app with a matching name rather than creating a duplicate, so re-running is safe.

constraints.validationMessage: Must contain {sub} so each subscription gets a distinct app name.

elements.name: permissionSet
elements.label: Graph permission set
elements.toolTip: All names are verified to exist as Graph APPLICATION permissions. Note that 'Security.Read.All' is deliberately absent from every set here — it does not exist as an application permission, nor as a delegated scope, and requesting it silently produces a gap.

allowedValues.label: Standard + Defender TI and posture extras

options.text: Standard (12): AuditLog.Read.All · SecurityAlert.Read.All · SecurityEvents.Read.All · SecurityIncident.Read.All · Directory.Read.All · IdentityRiskEvent.Read.All · IdentityRiskyUser.Read.All · IdentityRiskyServicePrincipal.Read.All · ThreatHunting.Read.All · User.Read.All · Group.Read.All · Device.Read.All

Minimal (4): AuditLog.Read.All · SecurityAlert.Read.All · SecurityIncident.Read.All · Directory.Read.All. Enough for Entra sign-in/audit plus alerts and incidents. No advanced hunting, no identity-risk detail, no device or group enrichment.

Extended (17) = the 12 standard, plus AuditLogsQuery.Read.All (unified audit via Graph) · ThreatIndicators.Read.All · ThreatIntelligence.Read.All · Policy.Read.All (Conditional Access posture) · IdentityRiskyAgent.Read.All (agent identity risk). Several need Entra ID P2 or Defender licensing; an unlicensed permission is harmless but returns no data.

elements.name: secretMonths
elements.label: Client-secret lifetime (months)
elements.toolTip: The workflow rotates a secret only when none exists or the existing one expires within 30 days, so re-running never breaks a live credential.

elements.name: rbacRoles
elements.label: Azure RBAC granted on each target subscription
elements.toolTip: This is the ONLY real per-subscription boundary — Graph application permissions are tenant-wide and cannot be scoped to a subscription.

options.text: Leave the event trigger OFF for the first deployment. Deploy, POST one subscription ID at the workflow, confirm the run succeeds, THEN enable it. A broken workflow wired to a live event source fails silently across the whole estate.

elements.name: enableEventTrigger
elements.label: Create the Event Grid trigger now
elements.toolTip: When on, an Event Grid system topic is created for subscription events so new and newly-tagged subscriptions onboard themselves.

elements.name: managementGroupId
elements.label: Management group to watch (optional)
elements.toolTip: Leave empty to watch the whole tenant root. Only used when the event trigger is enabled.

constraints.validationMessage: Up to 90 chars, or leave empty for tenant root.

elements.name: useTagGate
elements.label: Only onboard subscriptions carrying an opt-in tag (strongly recommended)
elements.toolTip: Without a gate, EVERY subscription that raises an event gets an app registration. The tag makes onboarding an explicit decision. A tag write also raises the event, so tagging an existing subscription onboards it.

options.text: The workflow reads tags from /providers/Microsoft.Resources/tags/default, NOT from the subscription GET — verified on a live tenant that the subscription GET omits the tags property entirely for a Reader-level caller, which made the gate skip everything. If a run reports skipped-not-tagged with an empty tagsFound, the identity cannot read tags and needs at least Reader on that subscription.
NO TAG GATE: every subscription in scope will receive an app registration with a client secret. That is a lot of tier-0 credentials created without an explicit decision per subscription. Reconsider.

elements.name: failureWebhookUrl
elements.label: Failure webhook (optional)
elements.toolTip: Teams/Slack/ASTRO incoming webhook notified when an onboarding run fails or consent verification falls short. Creates an action group.

constraints.validationMessage: Must be an https:// URL, or leave empty.

options.text: STEP 1 — Grant the identity what it needs. Key Vault Secrets Officer on the vault, and Owner (or Contributor + User Access Administrator) on each target subscription, because the workflow assigns RBAC there. Run: ./scripts/Deploy-AbstractAppReg.sh -a Grant -g <rg> -k <vault> -s <subscription-id>

STEP 2 — Test with ONE subscription before trusting it. ./scripts/Deploy-AbstractAppReg.sh -a Onboard -g <rg> -s <subscription-id>. A consent shortfall returns HTTP 500 with the exact verified/expected count and creates no secret, so nothing is left half-provisioned.

STEP 3 — Backfill and then automate. The same Onboard command onboards existing subscriptions; run it per subscription (or loop it). Once a manual run succeeds, redeploy with the event trigger enabled so future subscriptions onboard themselves.

STEP 4 — Audit what exists. ./scripts/Deploy-AbstractAppReg.sh -a Status shows the identity, its consent, every Abstract app and every secret with its expiry. -a Verify --app-id <id> re-checks one app and names any missing permission, so "consent looks fine but Abstract gets 403" is diagnosable in one command.

Secrets never appear in deployment outputs, workflow outputs or run history — the Key Vault write action has secureData set on both inputs and outputs. Read them from Key Vault, and give Abstract the value from there.
